tool.name: n8n
tool.tagline: Fair-code workflow automation with a visual editor, AI agents and self-hosting
tool.description: n8n is a workflow automation tool: you connect nodes on a canvas so that an event (a form entry, a webhook, a schedule) flows through steps that read, transform and send data between apps. It has hundreds of integrations, an HTTP Request node for any API, a Code node for custom logic, and LangChain-based AI nodes for building agents. You can use n8n Cloud or run it yourself with Docker, which makes it popular with teams that want control over their data.

concepts.name: What n8n is: workflows, cloud or self-hosted
concepts.summary: Understand what n8n does, how a workflow is built from nodes, and the difference between n8n Cloud and self-hosting.
concepts.why: Knowing what n8n is good at, and how it is offered, helps you decide how to start.
concepts.body:
Imagine every new website signup should be added to your mailing list, checked against your customer database, and announced in your team chat. n8n (say "n-eight-n") lets you build that as a **workflow**: a chain of steps that runs automatically.

Each step is a **node**, a box on a canvas that does one job: "Gmail: send email", "Google Sheets: add row", "If: check a condition". You draw lines between nodes, and data flows along the lines from left to right.

The first node is a **trigger**: the event that starts the workflow, such as a schedule or a new form entry. Every node after it reacts to the data it receives.

What makes n8n different from tools like Zapier:

- It shows the actual data at every step, so you can see exactly what each node received and produced.
- It has strong building blocks for logic (conditions, loops, merging data) and lets you add small pieces of code when needed.
- It is **fair-code**: the source code is public and you may run it yourself, under a license that limits reselling it as a service.

You can use it in two main ways:

- **n8n Cloud**: n8n runs it for you. Easiest start.
- **Self-hosted**: you run n8n on your own server or computer (usually with Docker, covered later). The free community edition has almost all features; paid licences add team and enterprise features.

This course uses n8n 2.x. Many older tutorials show 1.x screens, which differ in places such as how workflows go live.
takeaways: A workflow is a chain of nodes started by a trigger
n8n shows the real data at each step and handles complex logic well
Use n8n Cloud, or self-host the fair-code version yourself

quiz.q: What is a node in n8n?
options: One step in a workflow that does one job
quiz.explain: Workflows are built by connecting nodes, each doing one task such as sending an email.

concepts.name: The editor: canvas, nodes and test runs
concepts.summary: Find your way around the editor: add and connect nodes, open a node's input and output, and run the workflow manually.
concepts.why: Everything in n8n is built and debugged in the editor, so moving around it confidently saves hours.
concepts.body:
Open a new workflow and you see an empty **canvas**. Click the plus button (or press Tab) to search for nodes. Nodes come in a few kinds:

- **Trigger nodes** start a workflow.
- **App nodes** work with one service, such as Slack, Notion or Airtable. Each offers actions like "create", "get" or "update".
- **Core nodes** are general tools: If, Edit Fields, Merge, HTTP Request, Code, Wait.

Drag from one node's small output dot to the next node's input to connect them. Data travels along these connections.

Double-click a node to open it. You see three panels:

- **INPUT** on the left: the data that arrived from the previous node.
- **Parameters** in the middle: the node's settings.
- **OUTPUT** on the right: what the node produced the last time it ran.

You can view data as a table, as JSON (a text format for data, covered soon) or as a schema (just the field names).

To try things, click **Execute workflow** at the bottom of the canvas, or run a single node with its own execute button. Each run is called an **execution**. During building, executions use your test data and show their results right on the canvas: green ticks for success, red for errors.

Useful habits: rename nodes to say what they do ("Get customer by email" rather than "HTTP Request1"), add sticky notes to explain sections, and run often while building rather than all at the end.
takeaways: Trigger nodes start workflows; app and core nodes do the work
Each node shows INPUT, parameters and OUTPUT
Run the workflow or single nodes often while building
pitfalls: Leaving default node names, which makes later expressions and debugging confusing.

quiz.q: Where do you look to see exactly what data a node received?
options: The OUTPUT panel of that node
The INPUT panel of that node
quiz.explain: The INPUT panel shows the data that arrived from the previous node.

concepts.name: Trigger nodes: how workflows start
concepts.summary: Choose the right trigger: manual, schedule, app events, forms, chat or webhooks.
concepts.why: The trigger decides when your workflow runs and what data it starts with.
concepts.body:
Every workflow that runs on its own starts with a **trigger node**. Common ones:

- **Manual Trigger** ("When clicking Execute workflow"): only runs when you click. Good for building and one-off jobs.
- **Schedule Trigger**: runs on a timetable, such as every day at 8:00 or every 15 minutes. Check the time zone in the workflow settings.
- **App triggers**: many app nodes have a trigger version, such as "Gmail Trigger: on message received" or "Google Sheets Trigger: row added". Some are notified instantly by the app; others check for changes on a timer (called **polling**).
- **n8n Form Trigger**: n8n hosts a simple web form for you, and each submission starts the workflow.
- **Chat Trigger**: a chat window for talking to an AI agent (covered in the AI module).
- **Webhook**: a web address that any other system can call to start the workflow (its own lesson later).
- **Error Trigger** and **Execute Workflow Trigger**: special triggers for error handling and sub-workflows, covered later.

A workflow can have more than one trigger, for example a schedule plus a manual trigger for testing.

In n8n 2.x the old "Start" node no longer exists; use the Manual Trigger instead.

Important: most triggers only fire on their own after the workflow is **published** (made live, covered in a later lesson). While building, you start them by hand or use a "listen for test event" button.
takeaways: Manual, Schedule, app, Form, Chat and Webhook triggers cover most needs
App triggers are either instant or polling
Triggers fire automatically only after the workflow is published

quiz.q: You want a report built every Monday at 9:00. Which trigger fits?
quiz.explain: The Schedule Trigger starts workflows on a timetable.

concepts.name: Credentials: connecting your accounts
concepts.summary: Create credentials so nodes can log in to your apps, and understand how n8n keeps them safe.
concepts.why: App nodes can't do anything until they have permission to use your accounts.
concepts.body:
Before a Gmail node can send email from your account, n8n needs permission. That permission is stored as a **credential**: saved login details for one service.

You can create a credential from the node itself (the "Credential to connect with" dropdown) or from the Credentials list. Depending on the service, you either:

- **Sign in with OAuth**: a window from the service (for example Google) asks you to allow n8n access. n8n never sees your password; it receives a permission token instead.
- **Paste an API key**: a long secret code from the service's settings page. Treat it like a password.
- Enter a username and password, or other details such as a database address.

n8n tests a credential when you save it and tells you if it works. Rename it to say what it is for, such as "Gmail - support inbox".

How n8n protects credentials:

- They are stored **encrypted** (scrambled so they're unreadable without a secret key). Self-hosters must keep that key safe, as the hosting lessons explain.
- When you share or export a workflow, the credentials themselves are not included, only a reference to them.
- Many credentials have an **Allowed HTTP Request Domains** setting that limits which web addresses they may be sent to.

On n8n Cloud, some AI model nodes can run without your own credential by using n8n's built-in credits.

In teams, credentials live in **projects** or your personal space, and can be shared with colleagues without revealing the secret values.
takeaways: A credential is n8n's saved, encrypted permission to use an account
OAuth = sign in through the service; API key = secret code you paste
Workflows reference credentials; exports don't contain the secrets
pitfalls: Pasting an API key directly into a node field or a Code node instead of storing it as a credential.

quiz.q: You export a workflow to share with a colleague. What happens to the credentials it uses?
options: Only references are included; the secrets stay in your instance
They are included in plain text
They are emailed to the colleague
quiz.explain: Workflow files reference credentials by name and ID but don't contain the secret values.

concepts.name: Data between nodes: items and JSON
concepts.summary: Learn n8n's data model: nodes pass a list of items, each item holds JSON fields, and most nodes run once per item.
concepts.why: Almost every confusing result in n8n comes from not knowing how many items flowed into a node.
concepts.body:
Data in n8n is passed between nodes as a list of **items**. Think of an item as one row in a spreadsheet: one customer, one email, one order.

Each item stores its fields as **JSON**, a common text format for data. JSON writes data as `"name": value` pairs inside curly braces. Values can be text in quotes, numbers, true/false, a list in square brackets, or another set of curly braces (a **nested** object, like an address inside a customer). The example shows two items.

Under the hood each item wraps its fields in a `json` key, and items carrying files (a PDF, an image) also have a `binary` key. You rarely need to type this yourself; the editor shows it.

The key rule: **most nodes run once for each incoming item.** If a Google Sheets node outputs 50 rows, a following Gmail node sends 50 emails, one per row, each using that row's data. You don't need to build a loop for this.

This rule explains many surprises:

- "Why did it send 50 messages?" Because 50 items arrived.
- "Why did nothing happen?" Because 0 items arrived (the previous node found nothing).

The item count appears on each connection line and in each panel, so check it whenever a result looks wrong.

If you really want a node to act once regardless of how many items arrive, turn on **Execute Once** in the node's Settings tab; it then uses only the first item.
takeaways: Nodes pass a list of items; each item holds JSON fields
Most nodes run once per incoming item
Check the item count when results look wrong
pitfalls: Expecting one Slack message but sending one per item because many items reached the node.

quiz.q: A node outputs 12 items into a "Send email" node. By default, how many emails are sent?
quiz.explain: Most nodes run once per incoming item, so 12 items produce 12 emails.

concepts.name: Mapping fields with expressions
concepts.summary: Drag fields from the input into parameters, and read the {{ $json.field }} expressions this creates.
concepts.why: Expressions are how each node uses the data of the current item instead of fixed values.
concepts.body:
When you configure a node you usually want values from earlier data: send the email to this item's address, not to a fixed one. n8n does this with **expressions**: small formulas inside double curly braces, `{{ ... }}`, that n8n replaces with a real value when the node runs.

The easy way: open a node, find the field in the INPUT panel and **drag** it into a parameter. n8n writes the expression for you, for example `{{ $json.email }}`. Read it as "the `email` field of the current item". `$json` always means the current item's data.

Every parameter has a **Fixed / Expression** switch. Fixed means the text is used exactly as typed. Expression means anything inside `{{ }}` is calculated. Below an expression field, n8n shows a live preview of the result for the current item, which is the fastest way to check you got it right.

You can mix text and expressions:

- `Hello {{ $json.name }}, your order {{ $json.orderId }} has shipped.`
- Nested data uses dots: `{{ $json.address.city }}`.
- Small changes work inline: `{{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}`.

Because most nodes run once per item, the same expression gives each item its own value.

Expressions are written in a JavaScript-like style (JavaScript is the programming language of web pages), but you only need the simple forms above to start. The next lessons add data nodes and more expression tools.
takeaways: Expressions in {{ }} are calculated for each item
$json means the current item's data; dots reach nested fields
Switch parameters between Fixed and Expression, and check the preview
pitfalls: Typing {{ $json.email }} into a field left in Fixed mode, which sends the literal text.

quiz.q: What does {{ $json.address.city }} return?
options: The city of the first item only
The city field inside the address of the current item
quiz.explain: $json is the current item, and dots step into nested fields.

concepts.name: Saving, publishing and executions
concepts.summary: Understand n8n 2.x autosave and Publish, why production runs use the published version, and how to read past executions.
concepts.why: A workflow only runs on its own once published, and the Executions list is where you check what really happened.
concepts.body:
In n8n 2.x your edits **save automatically** within a few seconds, and each change is kept in the workflow's version history. Saving is not the same as going live.

To make a workflow run on its own, click **Publish** (top right). Publishing makes the current version live: schedules start, app triggers listen, and webhook and form triggers use their **production** addresses. You can name the published version and add a description.

Afterwards you can keep editing. Your changes stay as a draft, and production keeps running the last published version until you publish again. This replaces the Active/Inactive switch of n8n 1.x, so older tutorials that say "activate the workflow" mean "publish".

**Unpublish** takes the workflow out of production. Version history lets you restore an older version or publish a different one, which is how you roll back a bad change.

Every run is an **execution**. The workflow's **Executions** tab lists them with status (success, error, running, waiting) and time. Open one to see the data at every node, exactly as it was. Production runs are only visible here, not on the editing canvas.

Two settings worth knowing:

- Which executions to save (all, or only failed ones), which matters for privacy and disk space on busy workflows.
- The workflow's time zone, used by Schedule triggers.

Only one person can edit a workflow at a time; others see it read-only.
takeaways: Edits autosave; Publish makes a version live
Production runs the last published version until you publish again
The Executions tab shows the data of every past run
pitfalls: Editing a live workflow and forgetting to publish, then wondering why production still behaves the old way.

quiz.q: You fixed a bug in a published workflow and the editor shows your change. Production still has the bug. Why?
options: The fix is in the draft; you must publish again
Executions are cached for a day
quiz.explain: Production runs the last published version; draft edits go live only when you publish.

concepts.name: Edit Fields and other data nodes
concepts.summary: Reshape data without code using Edit Fields (Set), Filter, Sort, Limit, Remove Duplicates, Split Out and Aggregate.
concepts.why: Cleaning and reshaping data is most of the work in real workflows, and these nodes do it visibly.
concepts.body:
Data rarely arrives in the shape the next app wants. n8n has small **data nodes** for common reshaping jobs, so you don't need code.

- **Edit Fields (Set)**: add, rename or change fields, and optionally keep only the fields you list. Example: create `fullName` from `{{ $json.first }} {{ $json.last }}`, and drop everything else.
- **Filter**: keep only items that meet conditions, such as `amount` greater than 100. Items that fail are dropped.
- **Sort** and **Limit**: order items and keep the first N, such as the top 10 by score.
- **Remove Duplicates**: drop repeated items, compared by all or chosen fields.
- **Split Out**: turn a list inside one item into separate items. One order with 3 products becomes 3 items, so the next node runs 3 times.
- **Aggregate**: the opposite, gathering a field from many items into one list inside a single item, useful before sending one summary message.
- **Summarize**: count, sum or average, grouped by a field, like a pivot table in a spreadsheet.
- **Date & Time**: format dates and add or subtract time.

When should you use an expression and when a node? Expressions are fine for small changes inside one field. Data nodes are clearer for anything that changes the number of items or the structure, and they show their result in the OUTPUT panel, which makes debugging easy.

Split Out and Aggregate are especially important: they let you switch between "one item with a list" and "many items", which controls how many times later nodes run.
takeaways: Edit Fields adds, renames and drops fields
Filter, Sort, Limit and Remove Duplicates clean up item lists
Split Out makes many items from a list; Aggregate makes one item from many

quiz.q: You have 40 items and want to post ONE Slack message listing all names. Which node helps most before the Slack node?
quiz.explain: Aggregate gathers the names from 40 items into one item, so Slack runs once.

concepts.name: IF and Switch: branching
concepts.summary: Send items down different branches with the If node (true/false) and the Switch node (many routes).
concepts.why: Real processes treat cases differently: urgent vs normal, paid vs free, found vs not found.
concepts.body:
**Branching** means sending different items down different paths. n8n has two main nodes for it.

The **If** node checks conditions and has two outputs: **true** and **false**. Each condition compares a value (often an expression like `{{ $json.amount }}`) with something, using a type-aware operator: for strings (text), numbers, dates, booleans (true/false), arrays (lists) and "exists / is empty". Combine several conditions with AND or OR.

Because n8n works item by item, one If node can split a batch: of 20 orders, 5 go out of "true" and 15 out of "false", and each branch continues with only its own items.

The **Switch** node is for more than two routes. In **Rules** mode you add a rule per output (output 0: country is "US"; output 1: country is "DE"...). Turn on a **fallback output** to catch items no rule matched, so nothing silently disappears. In **Expression** mode, an expression returns the output number directly.

Tips:

- Choose the right data type. Comparing numbers as text gives wrong results (as text, "100" comes before "20").
- Check both outputs while testing; an empty branch simply doesn't run.
- The Filter node is the simpler choice when you just want to drop items rather than route them.

After branching you often want to bring the data back together, which is the Merge node's job.
takeaways: If routes each item to true or false
Switch handles many routes; add a fallback output
Use the correct data type in conditions

quiz.q: 20 items enter an If node; 6 match the condition. What happens?
options: Only the first item is checked
6 go out of true and 14 out of false
quiz.explain: The If node evaluates each item and routes it to the matching output.

concepts.name: Merge: combining branches and data
concepts.summary: Bring branches back together and join data from two sources with the Merge node's Append, Combine and Choose Branch modes.
concepts.why: Many workflows fetch data from two places and must join them, like a lookup across two spreadsheets.
concepts.body:
The **Merge** node waits for data on two or more inputs and combines it. Its modes:

- **Append**: output all items from input 1, then all from input 2 (and more inputs if added). Use it to rejoin branches after an If node.
- **Combine** with **Matching Fields**: pair items whose field values match, like matching customers from your CRM with invoices from billing by `email`. You choose whether to keep only matches, non-matches, or everything. This is the n8n version of a spreadsheet lookup (VLOOKUP).
- **Combine** by **Position**: pair the first item of input 1 with the first item of input 2, and so on. Only safe when both lists are in the same order.
- **Combine** with **All Possible Combinations**: every item of one input with every item of the other.
- **SQL Query**: write a query in SQL (a language for asking questions of tables) using `input1`, `input2`.
- **Choose Branch**: output the data of one input only, used to wait for both branches to finish.

Example: a Schedule trigger fetches today's orders from Shopify and all customers from a Google Sheet in two branches. A Merge node in Matching Fields mode joins them on `email`, so each order item now carries the customer's tier.

Gotchas:

- The order of the inputs matters for some options; check which branch goes into input 1.
- If one input receives no items, the result may be empty. Test with realistic data on both sides.
- Field names must match exactly, including capitalisation, or nothing pairs up.
takeaways: Append stacks items; Combine joins them
Matching Fields is a lookup between two data sources
Check input order and field names when results are empty
pitfalls: Using Combine by Position on lists that are not in the same order, which pairs the wrong records.

quiz.q: You want each order to get the matching customer's tier from another source, joined on email. Which mode?
quiz.explain: Matching Fields pairs items whose email values match.

concepts.name: Loops and batching
concepts.summary: Know when n8n loops for you, when to use Loop Over Items in batches, and how to slow down for rate limits.
concepts.why: Calling an app with hundreds of items at once can hit limits; batching keeps workflows reliable.
concepts.body:
A **loop** means doing the same steps again for each thing in a list. In n8n you usually don't need to build one: most nodes already run once per item, as you learned.

You do need an explicit loop when:

- An app limits how many requests you may send per minute (a **rate limit**), so you must slow down.
- You want to handle items in groups (batches) with the same steps, one group at a time.
- A node only processes the first item, or only runs once. Some database operations, and Code or sub-workflow nodes in "run once for all items" mode, work this way.

The **Loop Over Items** node (formerly called Split in Batches) does this. Set a **Batch Size**: with 1, items are handled one at a time; with 50, fifty at a time. Connect the steps you want to repeat to its **loop** output, and connect the last of those steps back into the Loop Over Items node. When all items are processed, the **done** output continues the workflow. It stops by itself, so you don't need an If node to end it.

To respect rate limits, add a **Wait** node inside the loop, for example 2 seconds per batch.

For "keep going until a condition is true" loops (such as fetching pages from an API until there are no more), connect a later node back to an earlier one and use an If node to decide when to stop. The HTTP Request node also has built-in pagination for the common case.
takeaways: Most nodes already run per item; explicit loops are for batching and special cases
Loop Over Items: steps on the loop output, connect back, continue from done
Add a Wait node inside the loop to respect rate limits
pitfalls: Forgetting to connect the last node in the loop back to Loop Over Items, so only the first batch runs.

quiz.q: An API allows only 60 requests per minute and you have 500 items. What's a good approach?
options: Loop Over Items with a small batch size and a Wait node
quiz.explain: Batching plus a pause keeps the request rate under the API's limit.

concepts.name: Expressions in depth: nodes, dates, variables
concepts.summary: Reference any earlier node by name, work with dates using $now, use helpers like $if, and read workflow variables.
concepts.why: Real workflows need data from several steps back, dates and fallbacks, not just the previous node's fields.
concepts.body:
`$json` only reaches the data of the node directly before. Often you need something from further back, such as the original trigger.

**Referencing other nodes.** `$('Node name')` reaches any earlier node by its name:

- `{{ $('Get customer').item.json.plan }}`: the plan from the "Get customer" node, for the item that matches the current one. n8n tracks which output item came from which input item (called **item linking** or paired items), so `.item` follows that link.
- `.first()` and `.all()` give the first item or all items of that node.

This is why clear node names matter: renaming a node updates expressions, but names like "HTTP Request3" make them unreadable.

**Dates.** `$now` is the current date and time, and `$today` is midnight today, both in the workflow's time zone. They come with formatting helpers from a date library called Luxon: `{{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}` or `{{ $now.plus({ days: 7 }).toISODate() }}`.

**Helpers.**

- `$if(condition, valueIfTrue, valueIfFalse)`: a quick either/or.
- `$ifEmpty(value, fallback)`: use a fallback when a field is empty.
- `$jmespath()`: pick values out of deep JSON with a query language.

**Context.** `$execution` (the current run, including its ID), `$workflow` (name, ID) and `$vars` (shared **variables**, settings stored once and reused across workflows, on plans that include them).

If an expression grows past one line, a data node or the Code node is usually clearer.
takeaways: $('Node name').item.json.field reaches earlier nodes via item linking
$now and $today with Luxon helpers handle dates
$if, $ifEmpty and $vars cover common needs

quiz.q: Three nodes after the trigger, you need the trigger's email field. What should you use?
quiz.explain: $json only sees the previous node; $('Node name') reaches any earlier node.

concepts.name: HTTP Request: call any API
concepts.summary: Use the HTTP Request node to talk to services that have no dedicated n8n node: method, URL, auth, query, body, cURL import and pagination.
concepts.why: With HTTP Request, n8n can work with almost any web service, not just the built-in integrations.
concepts.body:
Hundreds of apps have their own n8n node, but many services don't. As long as a service has an **API** (a documented way for programs to send it requests and get answers), the **HTTP Request** node can use it.

A request has a few parts, all described in the service's API documentation:

- **Method**: what you want to do. GET reads data, POST creates something, PATCH or PUT updates, DELETE removes.
- **URL**: the address of the resource, such as `https://api.example.com/v1/customers`.
- **Authentication**: prefer **Predefined Credential Type** when n8n already knows the service, so you reuse a normal credential. Otherwise use a generic type such as Header Auth (an API key sent in a header, an extra labelled line of the request) or OAuth2.
- **Query parameters**: options added to the URL, such as `?status=open`.
- **Headers**: extra labelled information.
- **Body**: the data you send with POST or PUT, usually JSON.

Shortcut: API docs often show examples as a **cURL** command (a command-line tool for web requests). Click **Import cURL**, paste it, and n8n fills in the node.

The response becomes items for the next node. Useful options: **Pagination** fetches page after page of results automatically; "Never Error" lets you handle failed responses yourself; batching spaces out requests.

The same node can also be given to an AI agent as a tool, with options to trim long responses so they use fewer tokens (the pieces of text AI models read and are billed by).

Never paste API keys into the URL or body; keep them in credentials.
takeaways: HTTP Request reaches any service with an API
Method, URL, auth, query, headers and body come from the API docs
Use Import cURL and built-in pagination; keep keys in credentials
pitfalls: Putting an API key directly in the URL, where it ends up in execution logs.

quiz.q: The API docs say "POST /v1/tickets with a JSON body". What does POST indicate?
quiz.explain: POST is the method normally used to create a new resource.

concepts.name: Webhooks: start workflows from any system
concepts.summary: Use the Webhook node to receive data from other systems, understand test vs production URLs, and send a response back.
concepts.why: Webhooks let other apps start your workflow instantly and even turn a workflow into a small API.
concepts.body:
A **webhook** is an automatic message one system sends to a web address when something happens: "invoice paid", "form submitted". The **Webhook** trigger node gives your workflow such an address.

Each Webhook node has two URLs:

- The **test URL** works only while you click "Listen for test event" in the editor. The incoming data appears in the node so you can build the next steps.
- The **production URL** works once the workflow is published. Its runs show up in the Executions list, not on the canvas.

Give the production URL to the sending system. Mixing the two up is the most common webhook problem.

Settings:

- **HTTP method**: usually POST (data in the body) or GET.
- **Authentication**: Basic Auth, Header Auth or JWT (a signed access token), so strangers can't trigger your workflow, plus an optional IP allowlist (only accept calls from listed computer addresses).
- **Respond**: "Immediately" (reply right away, then keep working), "When Last Node Finishes" (reply with the final result), or "Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node" (you decide exactly what to send back and when). Streaming replies are also possible for AI agents.

With "When Last Node Finishes" or Respond to Webhook, your workflow becomes a small API: another app sends a question and gets n8n's computed answer.

The incoming body, headers and query appear in the item, so the payload below would be reached with `{{ $json.body.customer.email }}`. Maximum payload size defaults to 16 MB.
takeaways: Test URL for building, production URL after publishing
Protect webhooks with authentication
Choose how to respond: immediately, at the end, or via Respond to Webhook
pitfalls: Configuring the sending app with the test URL, which stops working as soon as you stop listening.

quiz.q: Your webhook works while you click "Listen for test event" but not in daily use. What is the likely cause?
options: The sender uses the test URL, or the workflow isn't published
quiz.explain: Live traffic needs the production URL of a published workflow.

concepts.name: The AI Agent node: model, prompt and chat
concepts.summary: Build your first AI agent with the AI Agent node, a chat model sub-node and a Chat Trigger, and control it with a system message.
concepts.why: The AI Agent node is the center of n8n's AI features; everything else plugs into it.
concepts.body:
n8n's AI features are built on **LangChain**, a popular open-source toolkit for apps that use large language models (LLMs, the AI models behind chat assistants). In the editor they appear as **cluster nodes**: one main **root node** with smaller **sub-nodes** plugged into its bottom connectors.

The most important root node is the **AI Agent**. Unlike a fixed chain of steps, an agent lets the model decide what to do next, including which **tools** (actions it can call, next lesson) to use. Its sub-node slots are:

- **Chat Model** (required): which model to use, from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or models running on your own computer through Ollama. You need a credential for the provider (on Cloud, n8n's built-in AI credits may cover it). Model names change often, so pick from the current list.
- **Memory**: lets the agent remember earlier messages in a conversation.
- **Tools**: what it can do beyond writing text.
- An optional **output parser** to force a structured answer.

The quickest start: add a **Chat Trigger** ("When chat message received"), connect an AI Agent, plug in a chat model, and click Open chat. Each message you type becomes the agent's prompt.

The agent can also be fed by any other node, for example an email body, using an expression for the prompt.

In the node's options, the **System Message** sets standing instructions (role, tone, rules, what to do when unsure). Other options limit how many steps it may take (max iterations).

For simple one-shot jobs (summarise, classify), the **Basic LLM Chain** or Text Classifier nodes are cheaper and more predictable than an agent.
takeaways: AI nodes are clusters: a root node plus sub-nodes
AI Agent needs a chat model; memory and tools are added as sub-nodes
Use the System Message for standing instructions; use chains for simple one-shot tasks

quiz.q: Which sub-node must every AI Agent have to work?
quiz.explain: The chat model is the LLM that does the thinking; the others are optional add-ons.

concepts.name: Error handling: retries and error workflows
concepts.summary: Make workflows survive failures with Retry On Fail, error outputs, the Stop and Error node, and a central error workflow.
concepts.why: Published workflows run unattended; without error handling, failures go unnoticed until someone complains.
concepts.body:
Sooner or later a node fails: an API is down, a record is missing, data is malformed. n8n gives you tools at three levels.

**Per node** (in the node's Settings tab):

- **Retry On Fail**: try again a few times with a pause. Good for brief outages.
- **On Error**: by default the workflow stops. You can instead choose to continue, or to continue using an **error output**: the node gets an extra output, and failed items go down that branch, where you might log them or notify someone while good items carry on.

**Deliberate failures.** The **Stop and Error** node fails the run on purpose with your own message, for example when a required field is missing. That's better than letting bad data continue.

**Per workflow: error workflows.** Build a separate workflow that starts with the **Error Trigger** node and sends an alert (Slack, email, a ticket). Then, in each important workflow's Settings, choose it as the **Error workflow**. Whenever a production run fails, the error workflow receives details: workflow name and ID, the execution ID and URL, the last node that ran, and the error message. One error workflow can serve all your workflows.

**Afterwards**, open the failed execution in the Executions list, fix the cause, and retry it.

Design tip: make workflows safe to run twice (check whether a record exists before creating it), because retries and re-runs will happen.
takeaways: Retry On Fail handles brief outages
Error outputs let failed items take their own branch
A central error workflow (Error Trigger) alerts you about failed runs
pitfalls: Setting nodes to "continue" on error without logging, so failures disappear silently.

quiz.q: Which node must an error workflow start with?
quiz.explain: The Error Trigger receives the details of the failed execution.

concepts.name: Sub-workflows: reusable building blocks
concepts.summary: Split big workflows into smaller ones and call them with Execute Sub-workflow, passing defined inputs and getting results back.
concepts.why: Sub-workflows keep large automations readable and let several workflows share one tested piece of logic.
concepts.body:
Big workflows with 60 nodes become hard to read and test. **Sub-workflows** let you split them, like moving a repeated recipe step into its own card.

A sub-workflow is a normal workflow that starts with the **Execute Workflow Trigger** (shown as "When Executed by Another Workflow"). It defines what input it accepts:

- **Define using fields below**: name each input and its type, such as `email` (string) and `amount` (number). Callers then see exactly these fields.
- **Define using JSON example**: paste a sample of the expected data.
- **Accept all data**: anything goes, so the sub-workflow must cope with missing values.

In the parent workflow, the **Execute Sub-workflow** node picks the sub-workflow and maps data into its inputs. The data produced by the sub-workflow's last node comes back as the node's output. You can also choose to not wait for the result, for fire-and-forget jobs.

Uses:

- Shared logic: "find or create customer" used by ten workflows.
- Smaller pieces that are easier to test in isolation.
- Tools for AI agents: the **Call n8n Workflow Tool** lets an agent run a sub-workflow (next lessons).
- Memory relief: heavy work in a sub-workflow frees memory when it finishes.

In the editor you can select nodes and convert them into a sub-workflow directly.

Note for n8n 2.x: when a sub-workflow pauses (waiting for a webhook, form or approval) and resumes, the parent now receives the sub-workflow's final output.
takeaways: Sub-workflows start with the Execute Workflow Trigger
Define inputs explicitly so callers know what to send
Execute Sub-workflow passes data in and returns the last node's output

quiz.q: Which input mode makes the sub-workflow's expected fields clear to every caller?
quiz.explain: Named, typed fields appear in the calling node, so callers know exactly what to map.

concepts.name: The Code node (JavaScript and Python)
concepts.summary: Write small JavaScript or Python snippets in the Code node when built-in nodes get awkward, and know its limits in n8n 2.x.
concepts.why: A few lines of code can replace a tangle of nodes, but only if you know how items go in and out.
concepts.body:
Sometimes the visual nodes get clumsy, such as complex calculations or unusual text parsing. The **Code** node runs a short program you write. It supports **JavaScript** and **Python** (two popular programming languages). If you don't code, AI assistants can draft snippets, but have someone review them before production use.

Two modes decide how often your code runs:

- **Run Once for All Items** (default): your code gets every item at once (`$input.all()` in JavaScript) and returns a list of items.
- **Run Once for Each Item**: your code runs per item and works on `$json`, the current item.

Whatever you return must be items: a list of objects, each with its fields under `json`. n8n adds the `json` wrapper if you forget it, but returning the right shape avoids surprises.

Python in n8n 2.x runs natively through **task runners** (separate helper processes that run code safely apart from n8n itself). It uses `_items` and `_item` instead of `$input`, and needs bracket access like `item["json"]["price"]`. The older Pyodide Python was removed in 2.0, so old Python snippets may need updating.

Limits:

- The Code node can't make web requests or read files directly; use HTTP Request and file nodes.
- Reading server environment variables is blocked by default in 2.x.
- On Cloud, external libraries aren't available (JavaScript has `crypto` and `moment`); self-hosters can allow more.
- Never put secrets in code; use credentials.

If the logic fits in Edit Fields or an expression, prefer that: others can read it without coding.
takeaways: Choose Run Once for All Items or Run Once for Each Item
Return a list of items with fields under json
In 2.x, Python runs natively via task runners; no direct HTTP, files or env access
pitfalls: Copying a 1.x Pyodide Python snippet that uses dot access; native Python needs item["json"]["field"].

quiz.q: In "Run Once for All Items" mode, what should your code return?
options: A list of items, each with a json object
quiz.explain: The Code node outputs items, so it must return a list of objects with their fields under json.

concepts.name: Agent tools, memory and human review
concepts.summary: Give an agent tools (app nodes, HTTP, sub-workflows), let the model fill parameters with $fromAI, add memory, and require approval for risky calls.
concepts.why: Tools turn an agent from a chatbot into something that does work, and approvals keep that work safe.
concepts.body:
A **tool** is an action the agent may decide to call: look up an order, create a ticket, send a message. The model reads each tool's name and description, chooses one, fills in its inputs, reads the result, and repeats until it can answer.

Kinds of tools you can plug into the Tools slot:

- **App nodes as tools**: many app nodes (Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack...) have a tool version.
- **HTTP Request Tool**: any API.
- **Call n8n Workflow Tool**: runs one of your sub-workflows, the best way to give an agent a carefully controlled multi-step action.
- **MCP Client Tool**: tools offered by an external MCP server (MCP is a standard way to share tools between AI apps).

**Who fills the inputs?** Fix everything you can (for example the spreadsheet ID). For values only the model can know, click the sparkle button on the field, or write `{{ $fromAI('email', 'customer email address') }}`. The key and description are hints the model uses to choose a value.

Write clear tool names and descriptions; the model picks tools based on them.

**Memory.** Without memory each message is a fresh start. **Simple Memory** keeps the last few messages of a session; Postgres or Redis Chat Memory store history in a database so it survives restarts. Keep the window small: everything remembered is sent to the model each time.

**Human review.** In the agent's tools panel you can add a **Human review** step and connect risky tools to it. Before such a tool runs, the workflow pauses and asks a person (in n8n Chat, Slack, Teams, Gmail and others) to approve or deny. Denied calls are cancelled and the agent is told so.
takeaways: Tools: app nodes, HTTP Request, sub-workflows and MCP servers
Fix what you can; use $fromAI only for values the model must choose
Add memory for conversations and Human review for risky tools
pitfalls: Giving an agent a delete or send tool with every field left to the model and no human review.

quiz.q: What does {{ $fromAI('email', 'customer email') }} do in a tool parameter?
options: Reads the email from the previous node
Lets the model supply the value when it calls the tool
quiz.explain: $fromAI marks a parameter the model fills in, using the key and description as hints.

concepts.name: Vector stores and RAG
concepts.summary: Let an agent answer from your own documents: load and split them, store them in a vector store, and attach the store as a tool.
concepts.why: Agents only know their training data; RAG grounds answers in your current documents.
concepts.body:
Ask a model about your refund policy and it will guess, because your policy isn't in its training data. **RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation) fixes this: before answering, the system looks up the relevant passages in your documents and gives them to the model.

The lookup uses **embeddings**: lists of numbers that capture what a piece of text means, so texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. A **vector store** is a database that stores these numbers and finds the closest matches to a question, even when the wording differs.

**Step 1: insert your documents** (a separate workflow you run when documents change):

- Fetch the files (Google Drive, a website, a database).
- A vector store node (for example **Simple Vector Store** for testing, or Pinecone, Qdrant, Supabase or Postgres PGVector for real use) in **Insert Documents** mode.
- Plug in an **Embeddings** sub-node (the model that turns text into numbers).
- Plug in a **Default Data Loader** with a **text splitter** that cuts documents into chunks (small passages). The Recursive Character Text Splitter is a good default. Add metadata such as source or date to each chunk.

**Step 2: query.** Attach the same vector store to your AI Agent as a tool, with a description such as "Search the company handbook". Set how many chunks to return. You must use the **same embeddings model** as for insertion, otherwise searches return nonsense.

Keep chunks focused, return a handful rather than dozens (they all cost tokens), and tell the agent in its system message to say "I don't know" when the search finds nothing relevant.

Simple Vector Store lives in memory and is lost on restart: use a real database in production.
takeaways: RAG = retrieve relevant chunks, then let the model answer from them
Insert: loader + splitter + embeddings into a vector store
Query with the same embeddings model; attach the store as an agent tool
pitfalls: Inserting with one embeddings model and querying with another, which makes search results meaningless.

quiz.q: Why does the query side need the same embeddings model as the insert side?
options: Different models produce incompatible numbers, so similarity search breaks
Vector stores require one model per account
quiz.explain: Similarity only makes sense between vectors produced by the same embeddings model.

concepts.name: Self-hosting n8n with Docker
concepts.summary: Run n8n yourself with Docker: persistent data volume, encryption key, PostgreSQL, time zone, updates and HTTPS.
concepts.why: Self-hosting gives you control over data and cost, but you become responsible for keeping n8n safe and running.
concepts.body:
Self-hosting means running n8n on a computer you control, usually a cloud server. The recommended way is **Docker**: a tool that runs software in a **container**, a sealed package containing the program and everything it needs, so it runs the same everywhere. **Docker Compose** describes several containers (n8n, a database) in one file.

Key pieces:

- **Image**: the official package is `n8nio/n8n`. Pin an exact version tag (for example `2.43.8`) rather than "latest", so updates happen when you choose. In 2.x the release channels are called `stable` and `beta`.
- **Volume**: a storage folder that survives container restarts. Mount one at `/home/node/.n8n`. It holds the **encryption key** that protects all credentials. Lose it, and saved credentials can't be decrypted.
- **Database**: n8n uses SQLite (a single-file database) by default. For production use **PostgreSQL** via `DB_TYPE=postgresdb` and the `DB_POSTGRESDB_*` settings. MySQL is no longer supported for n8n's own data in 2.x.
- **Settings** are environment variables (named values given to the container), such as `GENERIC_TIMEZONE` and `TZ` for schedules, and `WEBHOOK_URL` so webhook URLs show your public address.
- **HTTPS**: put n8n behind a reverse proxy (a front server such as Caddy, Traefik or nginx that handles certificates), so logins and webhooks are encrypted.

Updating: pull the new image, then recreate the container. Read the release notes first, back up the database and the `.n8n` folder, and test on a copy for major versions.

You are now the operator: backups, updates, monitoring and security are your job.
concepts.code:
docker volume create n8n_data
docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 \
  -e GENERIC_TIMEZONE="Europe/Berlin" -e TZ="Europe/Berlin" \
  -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \
  n8nio/n8n
# then open http://localhost:5678
takeaways: Run n8n with Docker (Compose for production) and a persistent .n8n volume
Back up the encryption key and the database
Use PostgreSQL, pin versions, and serve over HTTPS
pitfalls: Running without a volume, so every restart wipes workflows and the encryption key.

quiz.q: Why is the /home/node/.n8n volume so important?
options: It keeps data, including the encryption key for credentials, across restarts
quiz.explain: Without it, restarts lose data and the key needed to decrypt saved credentials.

concepts.name: Scaling with queue mode
concepts.summary: Scale a self-hosted n8n with queue mode: a main instance, workers, Redis and PostgreSQL, plus optional webhook processors.
concepts.why: One n8n process can't keep up with heavy load; queue mode spreads executions across many workers.
concepts.body:
By default one n8n process does everything: shows the editor, receives webhooks, and runs every execution. Under heavy load (many webhooks, long AI runs) it becomes the bottleneck. **Queue mode** splits the work.

The parts:

- **Main instance**: serves the editor and API, handles schedules and incoming webhooks, and creates executions. It does not run them; it puts their IDs in a queue.
- **Redis**: a fast in-memory data store used as the **message broker**, the waiting line of executions.
- **Workers**: separate n8n processes started with `n8n worker`. Each takes executions from Redis, loads the workflow from the database, runs it and saves the result. Add more workers to handle more load.
- **PostgreSQL**: one shared database for all of them. SQLite isn't supported here.
- Optional **webhook processors** (`n8n webhook`) behind a load balancer (a server that spreads incoming requests) for very high webhook traffic.

Configuration essentials:

- Set `EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue` and the Redis connection settings on every process.
- Every worker and webhook processor must use the **same** `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` as the main instance, or they can't read credentials.
- Worker **concurrency** (parallel executions per worker) defaults to 10; n8n advises at least 5, since many low-concurrency workers can exhaust database connections.
- Binary data (files) can't live on one machine's disk; use S3-compatible storage (a cloud file store).

Enterprise self-hosted plans add **multi-main** setups for high availability.

Measure first: execution data pruning and lighter workflows often fix slowness before scaling is needed.
takeaways: Main instance queues executions in Redis; workers run them
All processes share PostgreSQL and the same encryption key
Use S3 storage for binary data and tune worker concurrency
pitfalls: Starting workers with a different N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so every credential fails to decrypt on them.

quiz.q: In queue mode, which component actually runs the workflow executions?
quiz.explain: The main instance queues execution IDs in Redis; workers pick them up and run them.

concepts.name: Versions, source control and environments
concepts.summary: Move workflows safely from development to production with Git-backed source control, credential stubs and one-way promotion.
concepts.why: Editing production directly is risky; environments let teams test changes before they go live.
concepts.body:
Inside one instance, **version history** already lets you restore and compare versions (n8n can show a visual diff of two versions on the canvas). For teams this isn't enough: you want to try changes on a **development** instance and promote them to **production** only when tested. Each separate n8n instance is called an **environment**.

n8n connects instances through **Git**, the standard system for tracking changes to files. A Git **repository** (a shared, versioned folder, often on GitHub or GitLab) sits between the instances. Typically each environment is linked to its own **branch** (a separate line of changes in the repository).

What gets pushed to Git:

- Workflows you choose, with their tags.
- **Credential stubs**: only the name, type and ID, never the secret values. You create the real credentials separately on each instance, under the same names.
- **Variable stubs** (names only), tags, folders, projects and data table structures (not their rows).

Recommended flow is one direction: build on dev, push to Git, pull on production. Don't push and pull on the same instance. n8n can't detect conflicting edits to a workflow, so a pull can overwrite local changes.

Pushing sends the **saved** version, not the published one. After pulling on production, publish the workflows there.

Permissions: instance owners, admins and project admins can push; owners and admins can pull. Source control is a feature of the paid self-hosted and enterprise plans. You can also automate promotion through n8n's API.
takeaways: Environments are separate instances linked through a Git repository
Credentials travel only as stubs; secrets are created per instance
Promote one way (dev to Git to prod), then publish on production
pitfalls: Pushing and pulling on the same instance and overwriting someone's unpushed changes.

quiz.q: When you push credentials to Git, what is included?
options: Only stubs: name, type and ID
quiz.explain: n8n pushes credential stubs; actual secrets are created separately on each instance.

concepts.name: Security hardening for n8n
concepts.summary: Harden n8n: SSO and 2FA, blocked nodes, task-runner isolation, SSRF protection, redaction, audits, and safe AI agent design.
concepts.why: n8n holds credentials to many systems; a compromised instance or a misled agent can do real damage.
concepts.body:
An n8n instance holds keys to many of your systems. Treat it like a sensitive server.

**Access**

- Use **SSO** (single sign-on with your company login, via SAML or OIDC) where available, and require **two-factor authentication** (2FA: a code from your phone besides the password).
- Give people the lowest role they need, and use projects to limit who sees which credentials.

**Instance settings** (self-hosted)

- Serve only over HTTPS, and keep the encryption key secret; replace (rotate) it if it is ever exposed.
- **Block nodes** you don't need. n8n 2.x already disables Execute Command and Local File Trigger by default, restricts file nodes to one folder, and blocks environment-variable access from the Code node.
- **Harden task runners**, which isolate Code node execution from n8n itself.
- Enable **SSRF protection**: limit which hosts and internal network addresses nodes may call, so a workflow can't be tricked into probing your internal servers.
- Disable the public API if unused, and consider **execution data redaction** so sensitive inputs don't sit in execution logs.
- Run the built-in **security audit**, which reports risky settings, nodes and credentials.

**Workflows**: protect webhooks with authentication, and validate incoming data with If or Stop and Error nodes.

**AI agents**: text an agent reads (an email, a web page, a document) may contain instructions written to manipulate it, called **prompt injection**. Give agents only the tools they need, fix parameters instead of using `$fromAI` where possible, and put Human review on tools that send, change or delete.
takeaways: SSO, 2FA and least-privilege roles protect access
Block unneeded nodes, harden task runners, enable SSRF protection, run audits
Treat agent inputs as untrusted: few tools, fixed parameters, human review
pitfalls: Re-enabling Execute Command on a shared instance, which lets any editor run commands on the server.

quiz.q: An agent reads customer emails and has a "delete record" tool. What reduces the risk most?
options: Human review on the delete tool and limiting which records it can touch
quiz.explain: Emails can contain manipulative instructions; approvals and narrow permissions limit the damage.

concepts.name: MCP: n8n as server and client
concepts.summary: Expose n8n workflows to AI assistants through instance-level MCP or the MCP Server Trigger, and use outside MCP tools in agents.
concepts.why: MCP connects n8n to the wider AI ecosystem in both directions, with real security implications.
concepts.body:
**MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and call tools provided by other systems. An **MCP server** offers tools; an **MCP client** (such as Claude Desktop, Cursor or an n8n agent) uses them. n8n can play both roles.

**n8n as a server: instance-level MCP.** An owner or admin turns on **Enable MCP access** in Settings. Assistants then connect to one URL for the whole instance (ending in `/mcp-server/http`), signing in with OAuth or an API key. Nothing is exposed by default: you mark each workflow (or a whole project or folder) as available in MCP. Connected assistants can search workflows, run the exposed ones, and in recent 2.x versions also create and edit workflows and data tables. Access follows the signed-in user's permissions.

**n8n as a server: MCP Server Trigger.** This node turns a single workflow into its own MCP server with specific tools attached. Use it for a small, self-contained tool set; use instance-level access for broad use.

**n8n as a client.** Give an AI Agent the **MCP Client Tool** to use tools from an external MCP server. Recent versions also offer some popular MCP servers directly in the agent's tools panel.

Design advice:

- Expose workflows with clear names, descriptions and defined inputs (sub-workflow style), not your whole instance.
- Treat every MCP call like a webhook from the outside: validate inputs.
- Assistants act on whatever they read, so keep write actions behind Human review.
- Revoke API keys and OAuth grants you no longer use.
takeaways: Instance-level MCP exposes chosen workflows to assistants through one URL
MCP Server Trigger makes one workflow an MCP server; MCP Client Tool consumes others
Expose little, validate inputs, and keep approvals on write actions

quiz.q: After enabling instance-level MCP, which workflows can an assistant run?
options: None until you publish to Git
Only workflows you explicitly made available in MCP
quiz.explain: Nothing is exposed by default; you enable each workflow, folder or project.
